activities.anchor: Three features to name before any modelling
activities.caption: read the graph — file each feature
activities.name: tsGraphSort

config.prompt: Three things to name on any plot, plus the traps — file each claim:

items.label: a strike, a heatwave, a change in how the data is recorded
an axis not starting at zero exaggerates slopes
electricity peaks every evening and every winter — two cycles coexist
a level shift mid-series often marks a change in measurement, not in the world

config.why: Is the seasonal swing roughly the same size every year (additive) or does it grow with the level (multiplicative)? The answer decides the model.

activities.caption: the café's three years — decompose in order
activities.name: tsCafeOrder

config.prompt: The café read, decomposed — order the components:
items: Takings rise slowly across three years — the trend
Spike every July, collapse every January — the seasonal, fixed period
A three-month crater in 2020 — the irregular
Compare this quarter with this quarter last year, not with last quarter
config.why: Naming the three parts first prevents the double error: crediting the July surge to 'our summer strategy' and blaming the January slump on 'this year's management' — both are the calendar doing what the calendar always does.

activities.anchor: it lags every turning point by construction
activities.caption: true or false — the smoother is not a forecast
activities.name: tsSmoothJudge

statements.s: The latest moving average is the forecast for the next period.
statements.why: It is centred in the past, undefined for the newest points, and lags every turning point — smoothing the past and predicting the future are different problems.

statements.s: A moving average of a rising series sits below the series.
statements.why: By construction — of a falling series, above it; the smoother trails the data.

statements.s: The forecast comes from the extended trend line plus a seasonal component.
statements.why: Never from the raw smoother — extend the trend, add the seasonal component.

activities.anchor: the seasonal pattern is what remains of the data
activities.caption: two models, one choice — pair each with its clause
activities.name: tsModelMatch

config.prompt: Additive or multiplicative — match each model to its clause:

pairs.right: value = trend + seasonal + irregular — deviations in units, summing to zero
value = trend × seasonal × irregular — components are ratios
'10% above the trend' — the right choice when seasonal swings scale with the level
actual minus seasonal component — the calendar's fiction removed so consecutive quarters compare honestly

config.why: Holiday retail doubling, not just rising, is the tell for the multiplicative model; same-size swings every year say additive.

activities.anchor: Forecasting with this toolkit is arithmetic
activities.caption: price the Q3 forecast
activities.name: tsForecastEst

config.prompt: Trend base 83.75, growth 1.5 per quarter. Seven quarters on, the trend is ≈ 94.3. Q3's seasonal component adds +10.25 — the Q3 forecast is about what?
config.why: 94.3 + 10.25 ≈ 104.5 — arithmetic, yes, but a single number masquerades as a certain one where honest practice reports an interval.
config.context: Extrapolation assumes the trend continues; structural breaks invalidate the whole decomposition.

activities.anchor: The mechanics above run inside every headline statistic
activities.caption: one line of this office's method is wrong — click it
activities.name: tsHeadlineSpot

config.prompt: One line of the statistical office's method is wrong — click it:
lines: Retail sales, unemployment and GDP are published seasonally adjusted.
A December-to-January retail crash reads as 'down 0.3% adjusted' rather than 'down 20%, because Christmas ended'.
The seasonal component is fixed once and never revised.
Money series are deflated into a base year — CPI rebased to 100 — so the trend is in constant purchasing power.
Comparing nominal sales across a decade of inflation measures the currency, not the business.
config.correction: The seasonal component itself drifts — holiday timing shifts, behaviour changes — so it is re-estimated continually; why a figure was revised is often the seasonal factors, not the economy.
config.why: A time series is never raw: by the time it reaches a chart it has been seasonalised, deflated, revised and re-based — ask which operations happened.

activities.anchor: removing seasonality means the seasonal pattern doesn't
activities.caption: the raw quarter vs the deseasonalised one — drag the divider
activities.name: tsDeseasonCompare

config.prompt: Same quarter, two readings — drag the divider:

before.label: the raw quarter
before.text: 'down 10% from summer, disaster' — the calendar's fiction read as management failure

after.label: the deseasonalised quarter
after.text: flat reads as flat — the calendar stripped out so quarters compare honestly; the summer surge is still real revenue and real staffing need

config.why: Deseasonalising is for comparison, not dismissal — the point is to stop attributing the calendar to the strategy.
